Do not worry, this pistol was not real.
Here is generous money for these inconveniences.
Thank you, we are glad to help our guests.
Runt, come here right now!
Chef, do you want to fire me?
Let us sum up your first work week.
On the first day you almost poisoned a guest.
On the second day you started a brawl in the bar.
You angered our chief art director.
And today you were almost shot!
Chef, I promise to work much better.
Looks like you fit right into the team!
Let us head quickly to work in our kitchen.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Agentive or instrument masculine noun meaning 'art director', declining across all six Russian grammatical cases.

examples.trans: I am the art director of the restaurant.
Vika works as the restaurant art director.
This is Viktoria Sergeyevna, our art director.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bar, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Our bar is closing.

examples.text: Проверьте все бары и старых друзей.
examples.trans: Check all the bars and old friends.
It is already morning. Our bar is closing.

meanings.note: Privative prefix 'бес-' ('without, -less', before voiceless consonants) (stem 'покоиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to worry', paired with 'забеспокоиться'.

examples.trans: Don't worry.
Mum is worried.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('here') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('! = you'll see!') (emphasis) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There, look.
Here's my toy car.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.en: to fit in, blend into a team or setting
meanings.note: integrate smoothly into a social group or environment

examples.trans: You fit into the team perfectly.

examples.text: Новичок быстро вписался в рабочий ритм.
examples.trans: The newcomer quickly blended into the work rhythm.

examples.text: Похоже, ты отлично вписываешься в коллектив!
examples.trans: Looks like you fit right into the team!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'second', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: This is my second term.
The second lesson is hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: As you all know...
Does the governor support you?

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'main' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('the main thing') (neuter главное, used as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The main thing is, don't worry.
This is the main street.
The most important thing is the people.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.
You have visitors!

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: Good afternoon!
I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: plural only: there is no singular in everyday use

examples.trans: I have no money.
The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'fight'.

examples.trans: A noisy fight broke out on the street.
Stop this senseless fight!
Stop this fight right now!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'стрелить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to shoot', forming an aspectual pair with 'застреливать'.

examples.text: Если шеф узнает про испорченный торт, он нас просто застрелит взглядом!
examples.trans: If the chef finds out about the ruined cake, he will simply shoot us down with a glare!

examples.text: Герой старого фильма грозился застрелить своего главного соперника.
examples.trans: The hero of the old movie threatened to shoot his main rival.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm going home.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'винить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to excuse', forming an aspectual pair with 'извинять'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to excuse, to forgive') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Sorry, I'm in a hurry.
Sorry, please.
Thank you, Marina. Sorry, I'm in a hurry.

meanings.note: concluding sum or recap of an event

examples.trans: Let's sum up the first week.

examples.text: В итоге все остались очень довольны.
examples.trans: In the end everyone remained very satisfied.

examples.text: Подведём итоги твоей первой рабочей недели.
examples.trans: Let us sum up your first work week.

meanings.note: all the people working together in an organisation

examples.trans: The staff forced me into this.

examples.text: У нас на работе очень дружный коллектив.
examples.trans: We have a very friendly team at work.

examples.text: Я своё мнение не менял. Это меня коллектив заставил.
examples.trans: I haven't changed my opinion. The staff forced me into this.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We're sitting in the kitchen.
Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.en: much, far, a lot (before a comparative)
meanings.note: намного хуже = much worse; намного лучше = much better

examples.trans: In prison it will be much worse.
Today is much warmer.

examples.text: Но я же вижу, как тебе плохо. В тюрьме будет намного хуже, поверь мне.
examples.trans: But I can see how bad things are for you. In prison it will be much worse, believe me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: This is real success!
He is a true friend.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: неделю = for a week; через неделю = in a week

examples.trans: I've been waiting a week.
The sea in a week!

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: trouble or disturbance caused to others

examples.trans: Sorry for the inconvenience caused.

examples.text: Шум в зале создал большие неудобства.
examples.trans: The noise in the dining room caused great inconvenience.

examples.text: Вот вам щедрые деньги за эти неудобства.
examples.trans: Here is generous money for these inconveniences.

meanings.note: + dative of the person: обещать вам

examples.trans: I promise you.
You promised!

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.note: playful derogatory nickname used by Chef Barinov for Max

examples.trans: Runt, are you still standing here?
The chef often called the newcomer a runt.

examples.text: Огузок, ты официально принят в штат нашего ресторана!
examples.trans: Rump, you are officially hired onto our restaurant staff!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.
Secondary conversational sense ('great!, excellent!') (as a one-word reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I know this town really well!
Everything went great.
Perfect, Vanya!

meanings.en: to poison, intoxicate with venom or toxic substance
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'равить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to poison', forming an aspectual pair with 'отравлять'.

examples.text: В первый день ты чуть не отравил гостя.
examples.trans: On the first day you almost poisoned a guest.
The spoiled dish could have poisoned people.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'first', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: This is my first day.

examples.text: Ты не понимаешь с первого раза?
examples.trans: You don't understand the first time?

examples.text: Ты что, с первого раза не понимаешь?
examples.trans: What, you don't understand the first time?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'pistol, handgun' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Stop, why did you take a pistol?
The officer put the pistol away in its holster.

examples.text: Стой, ты зачем пистолет взял? Ты что, с ума сошёл? Дай сюда!
examples.trans: Stop, why did you take a pistol? Are you out of your mind? Give it here!

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'вести'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to let down', forming an aspectual pair with 'подводить'.

examples.trans: I will never let you down.

examples.text: Надёжный друг никогда не подведёт в беде.
examples.trans: A reliable friend will never let you down in trouble.

examples.text: Подведём итоги твоей первой рабочей недели.
examples.trans: Let us sum up your first work week.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: May I go?
Let's go home.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мочь'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to help', forming an aspectual pair with 'помогать'.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Of course I'll help.

examples.text: Экскаваторщик — это не мой уровень. Может, поможешь?
examples.trans: Excavator driver isn't my level. Maybe you could help?

meanings.note: очень похоже = that's just like him
Secondary conversational sense ('it seems, looks like') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: That's just like him!
It looks like rain.

examples.text: Правда похоже. А может, вы сами позвоните губернатору?
examples.trans: It really is. Why don't you call the governor yourself?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'straight'.
Secondary conversational sense ('straight ahead') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Just like that?
Go straight along this street.

examples.text: В смысле, Виктор Степанович? Прямо так, да?
examples.trans: What do you mean, Viktor Stepanovich? Just like that?

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.trans: I work as mayor.
Where do you work?

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'working', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('worker') (as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: That means thousands of jobs.
A working day.

examples.text: Мы построим кластер. Это тысячи рабочих мест.
examples.trans: We will build the cluster. That means thousands of jobs.

meanings.note: short form only: рад, рада, радо, рады; no long-form cases

examples.trans: I'm very glad to see you.
She's glad.

examples.text: Ну что ты? Я очень рад тебя видеть.
examples.trans: Oh, come on! I'm very glad to see you.

meanings.note: provoke intense anger or irritation

examples.trans: You angered the chief art director.

examples.text: Его резкие слова сильно разозлили шефа.
examples.trans: His sharp words infuriated the chef greatly.
You angered our chief art director.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: I'm at home today.
I'll be there tonight.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: comparative of скоро used as adverb or particle

examples.trans: Let's go quickly to the studio!
Rather yes than no.
Bring the clothespin quickly!

meanings.note: спасибо за + accusative = thank you for

examples.trans: Thanks, Dad!
Thank you for your trust!

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: Give me the keys.
Come here!
The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: This is your coffee.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
Your boss is here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'волить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to fire', forming an aspectual pair with 'увольнять'.

examples.trans: You're fired!
He was fired.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.en: to arrange, organize, set up an event or scheme
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'строить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to arrange', forming an aspectual pair with 'устраивать'.

examples.text: Я всё устрою на высшем уровне.
examples.trans: I will arrange everything at the highest level.
They organized a party for friends.
To cause disturbances.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.trans: A good day.
What a lovely morning!

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'a little'.
чуть не + verb: я чуть не упал = I nearly fell

examples.trans: I nearly fell.
Wait a little.

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: Cleverly thought out, boss!
The boss signed the order.
The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'noise', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты можешь убрать весь этот шум?
examples.trans: Can you cut out all this noise?
Where is this noise coming from?

examples.text: Так, ты можешь убрать весь этот шум? Нам нужен только Аникеев.
examples.trans: Right, can you cut out all this noise? We only need Anikeev.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'generous', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: You are a very generous person.
Thank you for the generous gift.

examples.text: Извините, вы очень щедрый, а я неловкий. Я пойду попробую приготовить себе кашу.
examples.trans: Forgive me, you are very generous, and I am clumsy. I will go try to cook myself some porridge.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.
